explanations.answer: Buy grain so they can live
explanations.explanation: Jacob, the father of these brothers, says it plainly: “Go down there and buy some for us, so that we may live and not die.” (Genesis 42:2) Life is on the line, and the errand is just as clear. One job, friend, and it's buying grain. No side quests.

explanations.answer: Ask Pharaoh for land to live on
explanations.explanation: Land never comes up in Jacob's request. He tells his sons to go down and buy grain so that they “…may live and not die.” (Genesis 42:2) Pharaoh, Egypt's king, isn't part of the errand at all. It's a shopping trip, friend, just a very serious one.

Jacob says nothing about selling flocks. His words are about going down to Egypt and buying grain, so that they “…may live and not die.” (Genesis 42:2) Trading flocks for silver is a whole different business plan, and Jacob never pitches it. The plan on the table is one trip and one purchase.

Verse 3 says it straight: “So ten of Joseph’s brothers went down to buy grain from Egypt.” Ten brothers is a lot of people for one shopping list. Benjamin isn't in that number, as the next verse shows (Genesis 42:4).

Eleven is close, but it would count Benjamin, Joseph's younger brother. Jacob keeps him home (Genesis 42:4). The verse says ten went down. Counting is tricky when one brother stays behind and another is sitting in Egypt, friend.

Seven is a lucky number, baker, but it's not the one in the text. Verse 3 says, “So ten of Joseph’s brothers went down to buy grain from Egypt.” Seven would leave the group three men short. Ten is the number, and ten is a LOT of brothers on one road.

Verse 4 names him: “But Jacob did not send Joseph’s brother Benjamin with his brothers…” Benjamin is the brother Jacob keeps close to home. The ten go and he stays. You can tell Jacob has his eye on this one.

Dan isn't the name verse 4 gives. The text says Jacob did not send “…Joseph’s brother Benjamin with his brothers…” (Genesis 42:4) Benjamin is the one who stays home. Good guess at a family name, but the verse points straight at Benjamin.

The verse doesn't name Asher as the one who stays. It says Jacob “…did not send Joseph’s brother Benjamin with his brothers…” (Genesis 42:4) Benjamin is the brother kept at home. Keep that name handy, because he matters a lot in this story.

The flocks never come up here. Jacob gives his reason in his own words: “I am afraid that harm might befall him.” (Genesis 42:4) That's a father's fear, not a work schedule. Benjamin stays home because Jacob is afraid for him.
Right, nothing here says Benjamin is needed for the flocks. Jacob says, “I am afraid that harm might befall him.” (Genesis 42:4) The reason is a father's fear. No job posting involved.

explanations.answer: Bow with their faces to the ground
explanations.explanation: That's right. Verse 6 says that when the brothers arrived, “…they bowed down before him with their faces to the ground.” Joseph was the ruler of the land, the one selling the grain. Ten men bowing low in front of him, and verse 8 says they did not recognize him (Genesis 42:8).

explanations.answer: Ask to speak with Pharaoh himself
explanations.explanation: They don't ask for Pharaoh, Egypt's king. Joseph is the ruler of the land and the one selling grain, so the man they need is already standing in front of them (Genesis 42:6). What they do is bow down “…with their faces to the ground.” Nobody needs to go over his head when he's right there.

explanations.answer: Hand over the gifts from Jacob
explanations.explanation: No gifts in this scene, friend. The text doesn't mention any. What it says is that they “…bowed down before him with their faces to the ground.” (Genesis 42:6) They came to buy grain, and the man selling it was Joseph, the ruler of the land. Bowing is the first thing the verse shows them doing.

Verse 7 says Joseph “…recognized them, but he treated them as strangers…” He knows exactly who they are, and he plays like he's never met them. That's a lot of poker face for one man standing in front of his own brothers.

The text says Joseph “…spoke harshly to them.” (Genesis 42:7) His first words are a question: “Where have you come from?” That's not a friendly greeting at the front desk. It's a hard question from the man in charge.
Guests would get a warm welcome, and that's not what verse 7 describes. Joseph “…treated them as strangers and spoke harshly to them.” (Genesis 42:7) Not exactly a welcome basket, friend.

Gently is the opposite of what the verse says. Joseph “…spoke harshly to them.” (Genesis 42:7) There's no soft landing in this conversation. His tone is hard even though he knows exactly who is in front of him.

Joseph knows they're family, because he “recognized them.” But verse 7 says he “…treated them as strangers…” So on the outside it looks like strangers, and on the inside it's his own brothers. That's a whole lot going on behind one serious face.

That's the charge. Joseph says, “You are spies! You have come to see if our land is vulnerable.” (Genesis 42:9) He goes straight from a question to an accusation. The brothers came for grain and left that conversation with a spy charge.

Nobody calls them thieves in this scene. Joseph's word is “spies,” and he says they've come “…to see if our land is vulnerable.” (Genesis 42:9) It's a serious charge, but a different one. Stealing isn't what he says.

Rebels isn't the word Joseph uses. He says, “You are spies! You have come to see if our land is vulnerable.” (Genesis 42:9) The accusation is about looking over the land. Spies is the word, and he says it more than once.

The brothers say, “Your servants are twelve brothers, the sons of one man in the land of Canaan.” (Genesis 42:13) They count all twelve, even the one they say is gone. The man they're talking to is one of those twelve. He just heard himself counted.

Nine isn't the number they give. Verse 13 says, “Your servants are twelve brothers…” Ten of them are standing right there, so nine wouldn't even cover the crowd in the room. They give Joseph the full family count.

Fourteen is more than the family has. The brothers say, “Your servants are twelve brothers, the sons of one man in the land of Canaan.” (Genesis 42:13) It takes a whole lot of explaining to cover twelve. Fourteen would take even longer.

That's what they say. The brothers tell Joseph, “The youngest is now with our father…” (Genesis 42:13) They're talking about Benjamin, who stayed home with Jacob. That detail turns out to matter a lot in what Joseph says next.

The text says the opposite. The brothers tell Joseph, “The youngest is now with our father…” (Genesis 42:13) That means he's back home in Canaan. And that detail is exactly what Joseph picks up on next.

Joseph swears, “As surely as Pharaoh lives, you shall not leave this place unless your youngest brother comes here.” (Genesis 42:15) Pharaoh is Egypt's king, and Joseph uses his life as the oath. This is how he says the brothers will be tested. The test starts with one name: the youngest.
Joseph never asks for Jacob to come. His words are about “…your youngest brother…” (Genesis 42:15) Their father stays in Canaan. The one Joseph wants to see is the youngest.

explanations.answer: They pay for their grain twice
explanations.explanation: Joseph doesn't say a word about paying double. The condition is that they shall not leave “…unless your youngest brother comes here.” (Genesis 42:15) No extra charge on this receipt. It's about a brother, not about money.

That's the new deal. Joseph says, “…leave one of your brothers in custody while the rest of you go and take back grain…” (Genesis 42:19) That's a big drop from the plan where nearly everyone stayed locked up. One brother stays and the others head home.

Two is a good guess, baker, but Joseph's number is smaller. He says, “…leave one of your brothers in custody while the rest of you go and take back grain to relieve the hunger of your households.” (Genesis 42:19) Just one stays, and the rest head home with grain.

With ten brothers, half would be five, and that's not the deal. Joseph says to “…leave one of your brothers in custody…” (Genesis 42:19) One stays and the others go. That's a much smaller price than half the crew.

It's actually the other way around. Joseph says the rest of them should “…go and take back grain to relieve the hunger of your households.” (Genesis 42:19) The grain goes home with them. Only one brother stays behind in custody.

Right, they keep the grain. Joseph tells them to “…go and take back grain to relieve the hunger of your households.” (Genesis 42:19) The households back home need that food. The grain makes the trip with them.

explanations.answer: What they did to their brother
explanations.explanation: They say it themselves: “Surely we are being punished because of our brother. We saw his anguish when he pleaded with us, but we would not listen.” (Genesis 42:21) Their trouble in Egypt gets tied right back to how they treated him. They remember his pleading and say they would not listen.

explanations.answer: How they spoke to the ruler
explanations.explanation: That's not what they point to. Their words are about “our brother,” and they say, “We saw his anguish when he pleaded with us, but we would not listen.” (Genesis 42:21) They're not talking about how they spoke to the ruler. They're looking back at something much older.

explanations.answer: Coming to Egypt without a gift
explanations.explanation: A gift isn't mentioned anywhere in what they say. They say they're being punished “…because of our brother.” and that they would not listen when he pleaded (Genesis 42:21). Their minds go to the brother, not to a present. It's an old memory coming back hard.

Verse 22 says Reuben responded, “Didn’t I tell you not to sin against the boy? But you would not listen.” (Genesis 42:22) Reuben is one of the brothers standing there. He's the one reminding everybody that he spoke up.

Judah's a fair guess, friend, but he isn't the one speaking here. The text gives this line to Reuben: “Didn’t I tell you not to sin against the boy? But you would not listen.” (Genesis 42:22) I think this is a heavy moment, with years of regret coming out all at once.

Levi isn't the one speaking in this scene, friend. Verse 22 says Reuben responded, “Didn’t I tell you not to sin against the boy?” (Genesis 42:22) I think this one hurts. Reuben is reminding them that he warned them, and now they have to account for what happened.

That's right. Verse 23 says, “They did not realize that Joseph understood them, since there was an interpreter between them.” So they have no idea he understands. I think that's a very quiet kind of hard.

I'd lean True on this one, baker. The text says, “They did not realize that Joseph understood them, since there was an interpreter between them.” (Genesis 42:23) So they talk freely right in front of him. I think that's a lot to sit through quietly.
Verse 24 says Joseph “…took Simeon from them and had him bound before their eyes.” Simeon is the brother who stays. The others have to watch it happen, and I think that's a hard thing to watch.
Issachar isn't named here. The text says Joseph “…took Simeon from them and had him bound before their eyes.” (Genesis 42:24) Simeon is the one who stays. The other brothers watch it happen.

Zebulun isn't the name in this verse. Joseph “…took Simeon from them and had him bound before their eyes.” (Genesis 42:24) Simeon is the brother who stays in custody. The rest have to leave him there.

Verse 25 says Joseph gave orders “…to return each man’s silver to his sack…” So the bags get filled with grain, and the silver goes right back in the sacks. I bet somebody's in for a surprise when a sack gets opened.
A cup isn't in this order. Verse 25 says Joseph ordered “…each man’s silver…” returned to his sack. The silver is what goes back. Keep an eye on that sack for the rest of the passage.

No robes are mentioned in Joseph's order. Verse 25 says he gave orders “…to fill their bags with grain, to return each man’s silver to his sack, and to give them provisions for their journey.” The silver is what goes back in. The packing list says grain, silver and provisions, and that's it.

explanations.answer: Their hearts sink and they tremble
explanations.explanation: That's right. Verse 28 says, “Their hearts sank, and trembling, they turned to one another…” Finding the silver doesn't feel like good news to them. They ask, “What is this that God has done to us?”

explanations.answer: They blame the brother who found it
explanations.explanation: Nobody blames him. Verse 28 says their hearts sank, and trembling, they turned to one another. They said, “What is this that God has done to us?” (Genesis 42:28) They turn to each other, and they're shaken together. The question is about what has happened to all of them.

explanations.answer: They turn back to return it
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say they turn back. Their hearts sink and they tremble, and they ask each other, “What is this that God has done to us?” (Genesis 42:28) The next verse has them arriving home to Jacob. The trip keeps going.

explanations.answer: Their brother back and the right to trade
explanations.explanation: The brothers repeat the man's words to Jacob: “Then I will give your brother back to you, and you can trade in the land.” (Genesis 42:34) Their brother comes back, and they can trade there. It comes with a condition, which is bringing the youngest brother back to him.

explanations.answer: Free grain for the rest of the famine
explanations.explanation: Free grain isn't part of what they report. The man says, “Then I will give your brother back to you, and you can trade in the land.” (Genesis 42:34) Trading is the word, which means buying and selling. There's no free offer in his words.

explanations.answer: A place to live near the ruler himself
explanations.explanation: A place to live near the ruler sounds nice, but nobody offers a room with a view. The man says, “Then I will give your brother back to you, and you can trade in the land.” (Genesis 42:34) Their brother back and the right to trade. That's the whole deal, friend, and it only comes after the youngest brother shows up.
That's right. Verse 35 says that when they and their father saw the bags of silver, “…they were dismayed.” Jacob and his sons all feel it. Nobody's throwing a party over that silver, baker.
The text says otherwise. When “…they and their father saw the bags of silver, they were dismayed.” (Genesis 42:35) Jacob and his sons all feel it. Nobody's celebrating that silver.

Jacob says, “Everything is going against me!” (Genesis 42:36) He's just named Joseph gone, Simeon no more, and now Benjamin is on the table. That's a lot of loss in one sentence. I think he feels it all at once.

explanations.answer: This famine will be the end of us
explanations.explanation: Jacob doesn't say that. His summary is, “Everything is going against me!” (Genesis 42:36) He's talking about his sons: Joseph, Simeon, and now Benjamin. The famine is in the background. The heartbreak is right in front of him.

explanations.answer: I should never have sent you
explanations.explanation: That line isn't in the text. Jacob says, “You have deprived me of my sons.” and then sums it up with “Everything is going against me!” (Genesis 42:36) He's talking about what he has lost. Those are the words the verse gives him.

Reuben says, “You may kill my two sons…” (Genesis 42:37) That's a heavy thing to put on the table. I think he wants Jacob to see how serious he is about bringing Benjamin back. He also says, “Put him in my care, and I will return him.”
Flocks aren't what he offers. Reuben says, “You may kill my two sons…” (Genesis 42:37) That's a heavy offer, and it's about his own sons. It's a very serious promise.
That's not what Reuben says. His offer is, “You may kill my two sons…” (Genesis 42:37) It's heavy, and it puts his own family on the line. I think he's trying to show his father how serious he is.

Jacob says no. His answer is, “My son will not go down there with you, for his brother is dead, and he alone is left.” (Genesis 42:38) Reuben made his offer, and Jacob didn't take it. Benjamin stays put for now.

Right, Jacob refuses. He says, “My son will not go down there with you, for his brother is dead, and he alone is left.” (Genesis 42:38) Reuben made his offer, and Jacob's answer is still no. The story isn't over, though.
